q: Who was the first to propose and establish Psychology as the scientific study of behaviour?
who: N. L. Munn, the textbook definition of psychology

concept.t: "Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour" is the definition Indian textbooks quote from Munn, and that is what the key rewards.
Woodworth: the study of the activities of the individual in relation to the environment. Wundt: the science of immediate conscious experience.
Historically McDougall (1905, 1908) and Watson (1913) made behaviour the subject first, so read such stems closely.

wrong.a: Defined psychology as the study of the activities of the individual in relation to the environment, not as the study of behaviour.
wrong.b: Not a recognised name, perhaps a misprint for J. B. Watson, who made behaviour the subject in 1913.
wrong.c: Defined psychology as the science of immediate conscious experience, not behaviour.

q: Which branch of psychology focuses on the study of animal behavior?

concept.t: Comparative psychology compares behaviour and learning across species, so animal behaviour is its subject.
It grew out of Darwin's idea of continuity between species and Romanes' Animal Intelligence (1882).

wrong.a: Studies people in relation to one another, not animals.

q: What does clinical psychology primarily focus on?
who: Lightner Witmer, who named clinical psychology

concept.t: Clinical psychology assesses, diagnoses and treats psychological disorders.
The field was named by Lightner Witmer.

wrong.a: Belongs to industrial-organisational psychology, the applied field of work, not clinical psychology.
wrong.c: Belongs to comparative psychology, which studies behaviour across species.
wrong.d: Also belongs to industrial-organisational psychology, not clinical work.

q: In the nature versus nurture debate, which early philosopher argued that the mind was a "tabula rasa" or blank slate at birth?
who: John Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690)

concept.t: In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) Locke described the mind at birth as "white paper", with nothing written on it yet.
Every idea comes from sensation or reflection, so Locke stands on the nurture (empiricist) side of the debate.

wrong.a: Nativist: thought learning was recollection of inborn knowledge.
wrong.d: Nativist: held that the mind imposes innate forms and categories on experience.

q: ____ is a source of knowledge as per Empiricists.
who: Empiricism: knowledge comes through the senses

concept.t: Empiricism holds that all knowledge comes from experience delivered through the senses.
The rationalists (Plato, Descartes, Leibniz) put reasoning and contemplation first.

wrong.a: The rationalists' route to knowledge (Plato, Descartes, Leibniz), not the empiricists'.
wrong.b: Products of knowledge rather than its source.
wrong.d: Also a rationalist route: knowledge reached by thinking, not through the senses.

q: According to Wundt 'apperceptive mass' constitutes ___________ .

concept.t: The apperceptive mass is the organised body of ideas already in the mind, into which a new perception is taken up and understood.
So it joins a fresh pure perception to preexisting ideas; both halves are needed.
The term is Herbart's; Wundt reworked the idea of apperception.

wrong.a: The associationist and structuralist picture of the mind, not apperception.
wrong.b: Leaves out the existing ideas, which are the whole point of the apperceptive mass.
wrong.d: Helmholtz's theory of perception, not Wundt's apperception.

q: Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94):

concept.t: The trichromatic theory explains colour vision by three receptor types.
Building on Thomas Young's suggestion of 1802, Helmholtz developed it, hence the name Young-Helmholtz theory.

wrong.c: Helmholtz proposed unconscious inference in perception, but the unconscious mind belongs to Freud and, before him, to Leibniz and Herbart.

q: What do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common?
who: Ebbinghaus, Galton, Freud: lone pioneers who invented methods

concept.t: All three worked largely alone and were pioneers.
Each invented methods: Ebbinghaus nonsense syllables and the savings method, Galton the questionnaire, word association and correlation, Freud free association.
The RML 2020 key printed (a), but since (c) is also true, (d) is the more defensible answer and is the one the Panwar bank keys.

wrong.a: True, and the RML 2020 key printed it, but (c) is also true, so (a) alone is incomplete.
wrong.c: True, but (a) is also true, so the full answer is (d).

q: Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology?

concept.t: Wundt's Leipzig laboratory began research in 1879.
1879 is the conventional founding date of psychology as an independent science.

wrong.a: His laboratory (London, 1884) came later and was anthropometric, a centre for measuring individual differences.
wrong.b: A physiologist who founded no psychology laboratory.
wrong.d: Developed word association as a clinical tool in Zurich; no first laboratory.

q: Who gave the concept of 'Folk psychology'?

concept.t: Wundt's ten-volume Volkerpsychologie (folk psychology, 1900 to 1920) studied the higher mental processes through language, myth and custom.
Wundt held that these higher processes could not be reached by laboratory introspection, so he studied them through cultural products.

wrong.d: The physicist who discovered X-rays; there only because he shares Wundt's first name.

q: Charles Spearman is to Factor Analysis as Wilhelm Wundt is to:
who: Wundt, controlled introspection in the first laboratory

concept.t: Each pioneer is paired with his signature method: Spearman (himself a Leipzig doctorate) invented factor analysis.
Wundt made controlled introspection the method of the first laboratory.

q: Who among the following has defined perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal events?
who: Titchener, structuralist context theory of meaning

concept.t: For the structuralist Titchener, a perception is built from sensations supplied by the object plus images supplied by past experience.
This is also the heart of his context theory of meaning.

wrong.a: Probably Kimble, known for work on learning; he did not hold the structuralist definition.
wrong.c: Belongs to the New Look research of the 1940s, which showed that needs and values shape perception (Chapter 4).
wrong.d: Also New Look research (1940s): needs and values shape perception, not the structuralist definition.

q: The current approach to psychology most closely aligned with the structuralists in its interest in topics like consciousness, mental imagery and thought process is:
who: Cognitive psychology: structuralist topics, new methods

concept.t: Cognitive psychology studies the structuralists' topics: consciousness, imagery and thought.
It uses reaction times, error patterns and brain imaging instead of trained introspection.

wrong.a: Studies the brain rather than the contents of experience.
wrong.c: Banished consciousness altogether, the opposite of the structuralists.
wrong.d: Asked what the mind is for rather than what it is made of.

q: Functionalism, an early school of thought in psychology, was most closely associated with which psychologist?

concept.t: James's Principles of Psychology (1890) inspired the functionalist attitude.
Dewey and Angell turned it into a school at Chicago.

wrong.d: Functionalist in spirit, but Hall is examined for institutions (the APA, the first American research laboratory) and for adolescence.

q: Functionalism is how people work, play, and adapt to their surroundings. This viewpoint was given by:

concept.t: Functionalism asks how the mind helps us adapt: how people work, play and fit their surroundings.
That functionalist question is James's.

wrong.c: Inspired functionalism but belonged to no psychological school.

q: The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment.
who: Functionalism's Darwinian aim: the mind adapts the organism

concept.t: The functionalists studied the mind as an instrument that adapts the whole living organism to its environment.
It is the Darwinian question of what consciousness is for.

wrong.a: Reverses the order: the mind adapts the organism, not the other way round.
wrong.c: Narrows the subject to a single process, which is not how the school defined itself.
wrong.d: Narrows the subject to a single process (attention), which is not how the school defined itself.

q: The term "stream of consciousness", referring to the flow of thoughts in the human mind, was coined by which psychologist?

concept.t: In the Principles (1890) James argued that consciousness "is nothing jointed; it flows": a stream, not a chain of parts.
It was aimed against the structuralists' picture of consciousness as separate elements.

wrong.a: Known for analytical psychology and the collective unconscious.
wrong.b: Analysed consciousness into elements, the very picture James attacked.
wrong.d: A radical behaviourist who did not study consciousness at all.

q: The first person to use the term clinical psychology in print was

concept.t: Witmer opened the first psychological clinic in 1896 and proposed the new field that year.
He used the term in print in the first issue of his journal The Psychological Clinic (1907).

q: American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in:

concept.t: The APA was founded at Clark University in July 1892.
G. Stanley Hall was its first president.

wrong.b: One year too late; the founding meeting was in July 1892.
wrong.c: The tempting distractor: the year of Witmer's clinic and Dewey's reflex arc paper, not of the APA.
wrong.d: No link to the APA's founding; it only sits near the 1896 distractor.

q: Who among the following was the first female president of the American Psychological Association (APA)?

concept.t: Mary Whiton Calkins became APA president in 1905, the first woman to hold the post.
Washburn was first at something else: the first woman to earn a PhD in psychology (1894). She was only the second woman president (1921).

wrong.a: First woman to earn a PhD in psychology (1894) and the second woman president (1921).
wrong.b: Known for the psychology of women and of gifted children.
wrong.c: A psychoanalyst who was never APA president.

q: Who is often referred to as the "Founder of Modern Psychology in India"?

concept.t: Trained under Munsterberg at Harvard, Sengupta brought experimental psychology to India.
At Calcutta he set up India's first laboratory of experimental psychology (1915) and its first department of psychology (1916).

wrong.a: Bose is the father of psychoanalysis in India (1922), not of modern experimental psychology.
wrong.c: Not a founder of Indian psychology; perhaps a garbling of Sir Ashutosh Mookerjee, the vice-chancellor who backed the Calcutta department, an administrator rather than a psychologist.
wrong.d: Gopalaswamy began the Mysore department (1924), later than Calcutta.

q: Which of the following Indian psychologists played a key role in establishing the first psychology laboratory in India?
who: As keyed: Uma Chaudhuri; historically N. N. Sengupta (1915)

concept.t: The first laboratory was N. N. Sengupta's, at Calcutta in 1915, and he is not among the options.
Uma Chaudhuri of Calcutta, known for the Indian modification of the Thematic Apperception Test (1960), is the name the key expects.
If Sengupta is ever offered, choose him.

wrong.a: A later leader of indigenous Indian psychology (Section 2.8), not connected with the first laboratory.
wrong.c: A psychoanalyst and a later leader of indigenous Indian psychology (Section 2.8), not connected with the first laboratory.
wrong.d: Also a later leader of indigenous Indian psychology (Section 2.8), not connected with the first laboratory.
